title: Secondary storage devices
competency: Explain magnetic and optical secondary storage devices.

keywords.def: Auxiliary storage for permanent, long-term keeping of programs and data, e.g. hard disk, CD.
A copy of data stored in another place, used if the original is lost.
A metal magnetic disk fixed in the system unit; fast secondary storage divided into tracks and sectors.
A disk read and written with laser light, e.g. CD and DVD.

en.text: Secondary (auxiliary) storage keeps programs and data permanently, for the long term. Magnetic tape, a plastic ribbon coated with iron oxide, was the main storage in the 1950s–60s and is used today for backup: a copy kept elsewhere in case the original is lost. Magnetic disks, such as the hard disk, are the most widely used storage. They allow fast random access, and the disk is divided into tracks and sectors.

screens.title: A copy elsewhere
screens.ask: Why does a bank keep a copy of its records in another building?
opts: So data is not lost if the first copy is destroyed
screens.after: That copy is a backup, protecting against data loss from disasters.

screens.title: Magnetic storage
paras: Secondary storage is external to the main memory and keeps data permanently.
Magnetic tape: thin plastic ribbon coated with iron oxide; data stored by magnetising and demagnetising; used today mainly for backup.
Magnetic disk: round plastic or metal covered with magnetic material; random access, faster than tape.
Hard disk: metal magnetic disk fixed in the system unit; very fast access; divided into tracks and sectors.

Why did magnetic disks replace tape for everyday storage?
opts: They allow fast random access instead of slow sequential access
screens.ans: They allow fast random access instead of slow sequential access

screens.text: A song is in the middle of a long tape. Why is it slower to reach than the same song on a hard disk?
opts: Tape must be wound through in order; a disk can jump straight there
screens.ans: Tape must be wound through in order; a disk can jump straight there
screens.why: Disks allow random access and "solve the problem of slow access time" found in tape files.

en.text: Optical disks use laser light. Burnt spots (pits) and unburnt spots (lands) stand for 1 and 0. A CD holds about 700 MB: CD-ROM is read only, CD-R can be written once and read many times (WORM), and CD-RW can be erased and rewritten. A DVD (Digital Versatile Disc) has narrower tracks and holds 4.7–17 GB.

am.text: ኦፕቲካል ዲስኮች ሌዘር ብርሃን ይጠቀማሉ። ሲዲ 700 ሜጋባይት፣ ዲቪዲ 4.7–17 ጊጋባይት ይይዛሉ፤ ሲዲ-አርደብልዩ ደጋግሞ መጻፍና መደምሰስ ያስችላል።

screens.title: CD or DVD?
screens.ask: A DVD can hold a whole film, but a CD usually cannot. Why?
opts: A DVD stores much more data (4.7–17 GB vs 700 MB)
screens.after: DVDs have narrower tracks and hold far more data.

screens.title: Optical disks
paras: Laser light burns pits on the surface; unburnt parts are lands. Land = 0, pit = 1.
table: Read only: cannot write or erase
Erasable: write and erase many times
Digital Versatile Disc; 4.7–17 GB; narrower tracks
screens.note: A CD holds 700 MB, on one side only.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A disk read and written with laser light, e.g. CD and DVD.

screens.text: Match each disc with its feature.
DVD stands for Digital Video Disc.
screens.why: DVD stands for Digital Versatile Disc; "Video" is a common mistake.

screens.text: DVD stores larger amounts of data than CD.
You need a disc to save weekly homework, delete it, and save again next week. Which one?
screens.why: Only CD-RW can be written and erased many times; CD-R is write-once and CD-ROM is read-only.
